title: AI Valuation Reset Could Benefit Indian IT Firms, Senior Official Says
excerpt: As Nvidia's slide forces a reassessment of AI spending, a senior government official told Moneycontrol that moderating investment and a capital rotation could favour Indian IT services — with early FPI data mixed.
body:
• A senior Indian government official told Moneycontrol that Nvidia's stock slide and a wider reset in AI valuations could benefit Indian IT services firms, as clients moderate AI spending and focus on implementation and returns.
  • Moneycontrol's summary also said a capital shift away from concentrated AI trades may boost foreign inflows into Indian equities — a pattern already visible in early November FPI buying into IT and other index heavyweights.
  • The slide itself is not new: Nvidia is down more than 30% from its October 6 record and trades at about 12 times expected earnings, its lowest valuation since 2012, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.
  • For diaspora tech workers and investors, the near-term signal is client behaviour, not the headline: watch Nvidia's earnings on November 17 and Indian IT managements' commentary on AI deal pipelines.

The new development in the Nvidia story is not the fall in the share price — that slide has run for weeks — but an argument now being made in New Delhi about who benefits from it. A senior government official told Moneycontrol that Nvidia's stock slide and the resulting reassessment of AI valuations could benefit Indian IT services firms, and that a shift of capital away from concentrated AI trades may boost foreign inflows into Indian equities. Moneycontrol's published summary did not name the official, and the comments should be read as an official's assessment, not as a forecast or a result.

The logic: from building AI to proving it pays

The mechanism is a change in what clients buy. When AI valuations reset, large companies tend to spend less on indiscriminate infrastructure and more on implementation, integration, data engineering and cost optimisation — work that has to show a return, and core strengths of Indian IT providers. Analysis published this week made the same point: a shift from building infrastructure to proving returns may increase demand for that implementation work, even if weaker US sentiment also risks clients deferring some AI programmes.

What the market data shows so far

There is early, mixed evidence for a rotation. Foreign portfolio investors put Rs 53,739 crore into Indian equities in the first nine days of November, the highest monthly inflow since September 2024, after two months of outflows, with heavy buying in financial services, information technology, automobiles and telecom, according to the market analysis cited above. That followed a year of exceptional foreign selling — Rs 3.08 lakh crore withdrawn through October 12 — as the AI rally pulled capital toward the United States and semiconductor-heavy markets such as Taiwan and South Korea. A separate market report noted one session in which the Nifty IT index rose 3.3% as investors rotated toward services, adding about Rs 26,000 crore to Indian IT stocks' market capitalisation.

The counter-evidence is real. The same reports note pricing pressure and AI-driven deflation in traditional IT services, muted near-term prospects, and one brokerage view that India is unlikely to benefit materially from a near-term pause in the AI trade. India's 2027 earnings revisions were reported at negative 3.5%. A rotation in flows is not the same as a recovery in IT earnings.

The slide in context

Nvidia's fall is the backdrop, not the news. The Hindu BusinessLine reported that after a steep drop from its October 6 record high, Nvidia trades at the equivalent of 12 times expected earnings, its lowest valuation since 2012, is down more than 30% from its record, and was down about 12% in the week of the report amid the leadership scandal and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, with chief financial officer Colette Kress serving as interim CEO. Analysts on average still expect a 92% surge in October-quarter revenue and net profit of over $60 billion, up 89% year over year, according to LSEG data cited by BusinessLine.

"This is a key-person event, not a demand event. Nobody is cancelling GPU orders because the CEO resigned."

— Erik Kratz, Co-Head of Wealth and Chief Investment Officer, Arena Private Wealth, quoted by The Hindu BusinessLine

What to watch next

Two dates will test the official's thesis. The first is November 17, when Nvidia reports quarterly earnings and investors hear Kress on the outlook — the clearest signal on whether AI infrastructure demand is actually moderating. The second is slower: whether foreign inflows into Indian IT persist in the NSDL FPI flow data over the following weeks, and whether TCS, Infosys and their peers report AI implementation deals converting into revenue rather than price concessions at renewal. For Indian professionals in the US tech sector, that second signal matters most: a moderation in hyperscaler building does not automatically mean more services work, but a client pivot to returns, integration and cost control is precisely the demand Indian IT firms are built to serve.
